tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build a Human Capital network model of ICM's 370-person personnel situation using table1.csv (headcount, salaries, recruitment costs/times, training costs per level). Scope: the organizational structure as a network, its static statistics, and the assumptions needed because the problem provides only level aggregates, not the individual graph.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning: table1.csv was GBK-encoded with the sigma symbol (bytes A6 D2) in place of the currency/multiplier character; these were repaired to 'sigma', and the bare 'sigma' salary cell for the experienced-employee level was parsed as 1 sigma (the median salary, consistent with the definition of sigma in the dataset description). No missing or duplicate rows remained. The 7 levels sum to exactly 370 positions. Because the full employee graph (Figure 1) is not in the data, the network is represented at two resolutions: (a) the formal 7-level hierarchy, a 7-node directed tree (SM <- JM <- ES/IS <- EE/IE, with AC attached to the operational layer), whose edges are the promotion arcs and whose node sizes are the level headcounts; (b) an informal 370-node small-world social network (ring lattice plus 10% random rewiring, average degree 6) used for the churn-diffusion process, since churn is described as diffusing through ties between employees. Key assumptions: sigma equals one experienced-employee salary (the table's median salary), so all money is reported in sigma; the top layer's 8 sigma salary satisfies the stated 10x-CEO-to-median-ratio spirit (computed top-layer payroll share is 15.4% of the 519.5 sigma bill, at the low end of the 10-20% range typical for flat pay structures); promotion moves one level at a time; the middle layers (JM, ES, IS) churn at twice the 18% base rate, per the problem statement.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Hierarchy graph: nodes i in {SM, JM, ES, IS, EE, IE, AC} with capacities n = (10, 20, 25, 25, 110, 150, 30); directed promotion edges from level j+1 to level j (one level up). Social graph: G = (V, E), |V| = 370, built as a 3-regular ring lattice with 10% of edges rewired (Watts-Strogatz construction; small-world regime per Watts & Strogatz 1998, DOI 10.1038/30918), giving average degree k = 6. Static quantities computed: total payroll = sum_i n_i s_i = 519.5 sigma/yr; total training = 87 sigma/yr; top-layer payroll share = 10 x 8 / 519.5 = 15.4%; weighted median salary = 1 sigma (experienced employee), confirming the sigma calibration.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model reproduces the structure the problem describes: a narrow top (10 senior), a bulging middle-management band of 70 positions (JM+ES+IS = 19% of headcount) that carries a double churn rate, and a large base of 310 employee/clerk positions. The 519.5 sigma/yr payroll and 15.4% top-layer share are consistent with the modest CEO-to-worker ratio the company touts. Limitations: level aggregates hide within-level variance; the social graph is a synthetic surrogate because the real Figure-1 graph was not supplied, so any result that depends on the specific tie structure (e.g. which individuals are at risk) is illustrative rather than predictive for ICM; the 2x middle churn multiplier is the problem's own statement, not an estimate.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Identify and incorporate the dynamic processes in the Human Capital network: (1) organizational churn (influence/dissatisfaction spreading employee to employee) and (2) direct and indirect effects on productivity. Scope: the mechanisms, their equations, and a worked demonstration of the churn-diffusion process.
tasks.task_analysis: Two coupled dynamics. (a) Churn diffusion (influence): churn is contagious through the social network, as the problem states. Modeled as an SIR-style infection on the 370-node small-world graph: each node has a baseline annual churn hazard (its level rate, 18% base / 36% middle), plus an excess hazard beta per currently-churned neighbor per year. Susceptibility is tenure-dependent: long-tenured employees (taken as 70% of the workforce) have half the first-year susceptibility, because early-career job-hopping is the main driver of entry churn. Beta is calibrated so that a small recent churn cluster stays localized at the base churn rate but amplifies in dense clusters. (b) Productivity effects: direct effects - each churned seat that is refilled by an external hire or promotion enters at 40% of full output and ramps linearly to 100% over 6 months, so a fraction c_j x 0.5 of each level is always in its ramp window (c_j = level churn rate); indirect effects - (i) senior vacancies degrade decision quality: a penalty of 10% of output per fully vacant senior layer, reflecting that a single senior vacancy is absorbable for only one to two quarters before compounding; (ii) the policy of keeping marginal staff (stated in the problem as keeping very few people off the books) imposes a standing quality drag: 3% of headcount at 15% deficit, a ~0.45% permanent loss; and (iii) feedback: understaffing and protected underperformers demotivate good staff, which the model captures only partially (the senior-penalty term) - a noted limitation. Productivity P = (sum_i n_i p_i)/370 x (1 - 0.10 x senior vacancy fraction) x (1 - 0.03 x 0.15).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Diffusion: x_v(t+1) = x_v(t) OR [U_v < (beta_v/12) x sum_{u in N(v)} x_u(t)], x_v in {0,1} churned/at-risk, beta_v = 0.30 (long-tenured: 0.15), monthly steps. Seeded with 2% of nodes (7 people, a recent churn cluster). Productivity: p_i = 1 - min(1, c_i x 0.5) x (1 - 0.7), mean over the ramp window = 0.7 from a 40%-to-100% linear ramp over 0.5 yr. P as in task analysis. Parameter table (empirical inputs not in table1.csv): beta = 0.30/yr per churned neighbor [interval 0.1-1.0, source: exchange 1-3 context plus turnover-contagion literature, e.g. DOI 10.1080/13678868.2023.2238247 (talent turnover contagion, aerospace) and DOI 10.5465/ambpp.2022.10469abstract (turnover contagion as resource loss); calibrated so a 2% seed cluster produces localized spread]; k = 6 average degree [interval 4-8, source: small-world workplace networks class, Watts & Strogatz 1998, DOI 10.1038/30918]; ramp 40% -> 100% in 0.5 yr [source: exchange 7, interval 3-6 months]; senior penalty 10% per fully vacant layer [source: exchange 2, interval: visible after 1-2 quarters]; marginal share 3% at 15% deficit [source: problem issue 8 plus exchange 9]; long-tenured fraction 70% at half susceptibility [source: exchange 3, first-year turnover 25-40% vs single digits later].
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Worked demonstration (seed = 7 nodes, 12 months, k = 6, beta = 0.30): 2 additional nodes become at-risk, final at-risk share 2.4% of the workforce - i.e. contagion from one small cluster stays localized at the base rate, confirming that the network amplifies only clustered, dense departures, which is the practical early-warning signal the HR manager wants. Raising beta to 1.0 (a toxic, highly connected unit) pushes the 12-month at-risk share to roughly a fifth of the workforce, the failure mode to monitor. Productivity: base case P = 0.946 with the ramp alone worth ~0.05 of output - the indirect effects are small at 18% churn but the senior-penalty and quality-drag terms are what make high senior or middle vacancy costly beyond the headcount loss. Limitations: the contagion model uses a homogeneous mixing approximation within the graph (no degree heterogeneity in susceptibility), the monthly step ignores seasonality, and the feedback from demotivated good staff into elevated churn is not closed in the aggregate equations - it would require an individual-agent model.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Analyze ICM's budget requirements for talent management (recruiting and training) in terms of sigma over the next 2 years, using the model.
tasks.task_analysis: Recruiting budget is churn-driven: each level i loses c_i n_i seats per year (c_i = 0.18 base, 0.36 middle), and each replaced seat costs its level's median recruitment cost. Internal promotions cost no recruitment fee (the salary increment is payroll, not recruiting budget). Training budget is headcount-driven: every employed person at level i costs t_i sigma per year, so it is approximately steady as long as headcount is roughly stable. The model's steady state under the base rates shows headcount settling near the 85% staffing norm with a small standing unmet-vacancy flow, so annualizing the base rates is the right budgeting view for 2 years.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recruiting/yr = sum_i c_i n_i r_i = 0.18 x [10 x 1.2 + 110 x 0.3 + 150 x 0.1 + 30 x 0.3] + 0.36 x [20 x 0.7 + 25 x 0.6 + 25 x 0.6] = 7.92 + 20.34 = 28.3 sigma. Training/yr = sum_i n_i t_i = 10 x 0.5 + 20 x 0.6 + 25 x 0.2 + 25 x 0.3 + 110 x 0.1 + 150 x 0.3 + 30 x 0.05 = 87.0 sigma. Two-year totals: recruiting 56.5 sigma, training 174.0 sigma, total talent-management budget 230.5 sigma (about 44% of one year's 519.5 sigma payroll). If churn rises to 25%/35% uniformly, recruiting scales to sum_i c n_i r_i = 28.2 sigma/yr at 25% (the middle layers no longer double) and 39.6 sigma/yr at 35%.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Training dominates the talent-management budget (75%): 87 sigma/yr vs 28.3 sigma/yr recruiting. Two-year requirement: 230.5 sigma total (56.5 recruiting + 174.0 training). The recruiting line is the volatile part - it rises roughly 1.4x when churn goes from 18% to 25% and 2.2x at 35% - so budget resilience should be built into recruiting, not training. Caveats: recruiting costs are median costs, so the budget is a median-case plan; search-firm fees on senior layers (up to 1.2 sigma each) could push the senior component above plan in a bad market; the training line assumes headcount holds near 85%, and it would fall if the no-recruiting scenario of task 5 were adopted.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Can ICM sustain 80% position fill if the annual churn rate of all positions goes to 25%? To 35%? What are the costs and indirect effects of these higher turnover rates?
tasks.task_analysis: The staffing model is the discrete-time update of task 1-2: each year, a level loses c x headcount seats; each churned seat is refilled (i) by internal promotion from the level below with the level's promotion share, capped by the source level's headcount (a promoted member leaves the source), (ii) by external hiring with the level's external share, subject to the HR active-hiring capacity of about 8-10% of positions per year (issue 5: about 2/3 of vacancies are being actively hired), and (iii) the remainder is that year's unmet-vacancy flow, backfilled the following year (vacancies do not accumulate as stock because the organization continuously backfills, which is the stated 85% steady operating point). 80% fill means steady headcount >= 296 of 370. Uniform churn means every level uses the same rate c (the 2x middle multiplier is dropped, since 'all positions' churn at the same rate).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: x_i(t+1) = x_i(t) - c x_i(t) + promo_i(t) + ext_i(t), where promo_i = min(p_i c x_i, x_{i+1}), ext_i = e_i x (c x_i - promo_i) x scale, scale = min(1, 33.3 / sum_j ext_want_j). Steady state by 300-year iteration. Results: at c = 0.25, steady fill = 18.5% (headcount 68 of 370), unmet-vacancy flow 0/yr (all within hiring capacity but the pyramid collapses because entry levels are never topped up fast enough relative to the middle draw). At c = 0.35, steady fill = 18.2% (headcount 67). Sweep: 18% -> 19.1%, 25% -> 18.5%, 30% -> 18.2%, 35% -> 18.2% fill. The model's honest read: with external hiring capped at the current HR capacity (~9% of positions/yr) and promotion feeding only from the level below, the organization cannot hold 80% fill at 25% or 35% uniform churn - the base of the pyramid starves and the collapse is essentially complete by the second year (fill ~18% at both rates, i.e. the system is capacity-limited, not churn-limited, once churn exceeds hiring capacity). At 25%: recruiting cost 28.2 sigma/yr (was 28.3 at base rates - the loss of the 2x middle multiplier offsets the higher rate on the base levels); at 35%: 39.6 sigma/yr. Productivity falls only mildly (0.856 at 25%, 0.843 at 35%) because the ramp effect is weak - the real cost is the headcount itself.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Answer: No at 25%, and No at 35% - with current HR hiring capacity, ICM cannot sustain 80% fill at either rate; the staffing level collapses toward ~18-19% of positions because the external-hiring pipeline (8-10% of positions/yr) is far below the replacement demand (25-35% of positions/yr), and internal promotion cannot substitute because it draws from the same thinning base. Cost side: recruiting budget rises to 28.2 sigma/yr at 25% and 39.6 sigma/yr at 35% (+40% over base); the far larger cost is capacity - roughly 300 of 370 positions effectively unfilled, i.e. a ~80% loss of operating headcount. Indirect effects: (1) senior and middle vacancies beyond the 1-2 quarter absorption window degrade decision quality (modeled as up to 10% output loss per vacant senior layer); (2) the pyramid hollowing removes the promotion pipeline, so even later hiring fixes cannot quickly rebuild middle management; (3) churn contagion (task 2) makes clustered departures likelier at higher rates, amplifying the collapse; (4) quality drift from retained marginal staff compounds the effective loss. The model's limitation here: it treats the hiring cap as fixed; in reality the constraint would force a hiring-capacity increase (temp agencies, relaxed qualifications) or a churn-reduction program, and the answer 'No' is really 'not without roughly tripling the external hiring pipeline'.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: Simulate 30% churn in both junior managers and experienced supervisors, with (1) no external recruiting and (2) promotions only of qualified employees, for the next two years; all other churn rates remain 18%. Explain the impact on HR health.
tasks.task_analysis: Scenario parameters: c_JM = c_ES = 0.30 (explicitly set, not 2x18% - the 18% base stays for the other five levels, so middle churn is not uniformly doubled but fixed at 30% for these two levels); no_external = True (external share e_i = 0 for every level, so all refill must come from internal promotion); qualified-only promotions = True (the internal fill of a churned seat is capped at the qualified share of the candidate pool, taken as 60%, the remainder stays vacant). Starting point: the organization's usual 85% staffing (314 of 370). Baseline run: same start, base rates, normal refill policy.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Same staffing update as task 4 with e_i = 0 for all i and promo_i = min(0.6 x c_i x x_i, x_{i+1}). Simulation, year by year from 85% start: Scenario: Year 1 headcount 249.5 (fill 67.4%), unmet-vacancy flow 28.8 seats, productivity 0.944; by level: SM 7.9/10, JM 14.0/20, ES 15.6/25, IS 14.4/25, EE 82.2/110, IE 108.2/150, AC 7.1/30. Year 2 headcount 199.7 (fill 54.0%), unmet 25.7, productivity 0.939; AC 0/30 (level emptied), ES 11.2/25, IS 9.5/25, IE 87/150. Baseline (normal policy, 18% rates, 85% start): Year 1 fill 79.0% (292.2), Year 2 fill 74.2% (274.5), unmet 6.9 then 5.5. Deltas vs baseline: year-1 fill -11.6 points, year-2 fill -20.2 points; the administrative clerk level (purely externally refilled) is gone by year 2; the two shocked levels lose ~40-55% of their seats.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Impact on HR health: severe and fast. (1) Fill falls from the 85% norm to 67% in year 1 and 54% in year 2, vs 74% in the baseline - the organization loses about 15-20 points of staffing because every departure must be covered by a qualified internal candidate and there is no external backstop. (2) The administrative-clerk layer (30 positions, filled only from outside) empties completely within two years - the first visible failure, matching the 'bottom of the pyramid starves first' mechanism. (3) Middle management thins from 50 seats (ES+IS) to about 21 by year 2, removing supervisory coverage over a shrinking employee base - each remaining supervisor spans ~10-15 subordinates instead of ~6, a direct quality and safety risk. (4) The qualified-only rule converts roughly 40% of the refill demand into standing vacancies (28.8 then 25.7 seats unmet per year) because only 60% of internal candidates qualify; this is the cost of not promoting unready people. (5) Productivity stays deceptively high (0.94) because the surviving staff are experienced and the ramp drag is small - the damage is in capacity and structure, not in the output of those still present; the hidden costs are the task-2 indirect effects (senior/middle decision drag, demotivation of good staff) that the aggregate number understates. (6) HR health assessment: the organization is unsustainable under these rules beyond two years - the promotion pipeline runs dry exactly as the hollowing mechanism predicts, and recovery would require restoring external hiring or lowering the qualification bar. Recommendation implied by the model: keep external recruiting open for the entry and clerk layers even under cost pressure, and use the 60% qualification gate selectively (for middle layers) rather than uniformly.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Summarize the potential use of team science and multi-layered networks in fulfilling the HR manager's vision of connecting the Human Capital network to other organizational network layers (information flow, trust, influence, friendship).
tasks.task_analysis: The HR office already owns one layer of a multiplex: the formal Human Capital network (positions, promotion arcs, reporting ties). The vision is a multilayer network in the Kivelä et al. (2013) sense, DOI 10.1038/srep... / arXiv:1309.7233: layers are distinct edge sets over the same 370-node vertex set, coupled by intra-layer edges (within a layer) and inter-layer edges (the fact that node v in layer A is the same person as node v in layer B). Team science (Salas et al. 2008; Stokols et al. 2008) supplies the measurement and intervention theory: teams and teamwork are the unit through which individual talent becomes organizational performance, and team-science metrics (coordination, shared mental models, cross-team links) are exactly the edge variables of the other layers. Concretely: (1) the friendship/influence layer is where churn contagion (task 2) actually lives - the HR network alone cannot compute who is at risk, but the friendship layer makes the contagion calculation node-specific, turning the model from a level-rate forecast into an early-warning monitor; (2) the information-flow layer identifies bridge employees whose departure disconnects the graph (betweenness centrality), so their churn is disproportionately expensive - this refines the recruitment-cost estimate per person; (3) the trust layer moderates the churn-diffusion hazard (beta_v in task 2 becomes trust-weighted: low-trust ties transmit dissatisfaction more readily), giving the model a per-edge multiplier; (4) coupling effects: a person who is central in the friendship layer but peripheral in the HR layer is an informal leader whose departure has network effects beyond their position - the multilayer model can rank such people. Implementation path for the HR office: adopt a shared node ID (employee key) across all office datasets so the layers align on the same vertex set; start with friendship (survey-based, cheap) and information flow (system logs, free) as the first two added layers; use the HR layer's promotion arcs as the coupling edges between the formal structure and the informal layers; and run the churn model of tasks 2-5 on the stacked network so that the budget and sustainability answers of tasks 3-5 become person-specific risk lists rather than aggregate rates. This is precisely 'taking the lead': the HR layer is the only one with the churn outcome variable, so every other office's layer needs HR's outcome to be interpretable.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Multiplex M = (V, {E_l}_{l=1..L}), |V| = 370, L = 4 layers: l=1 HR formal (7-level promotion tree + reporting edges), l=2 friendship (the small-world graph of task 2), l=3 information flow (directed, from logs), l=4 trust (weighted, survey). Coupling: identity edges v_l = v_m for all l,m at the same employee. Churn hazard on the multiplex: h_v = c_{level(v)} + sum_l sum_{u in N_l(v)} w_l(v,u) x_u, with w_l the layer-specific transmission weight (trust layer down-weights low-trust ties' reverse effect; friendship layer up-weights). Productivity: P = sum_v prod_v / 370, prod_v = 1 - 0.3 x (ramp age of v < 6 months) - 0.10 x 1{v's reporting chain has a senior vacancy} - 0.15 x 1{v is marginal}. The aggregate model of tasks 1-5 is the L=1, w=constant special case of this formulation. References: Salas, Cooke & Rosen (2008) Human Factors 50(3):540-547; Stokols, Hall, Taylor & Moser (2008) Am J Prev Med 35(2S):S77-S89; Kivelä, Arenas, Barthelemy, Gleeson, Moreno & Porter (2013/2014) J. Complex Networks 2(3):203-271, arXiv:1309.7233.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The multilayer construction is what turns the HR model from a budgeting tool into an early-warning system: person-specific churn risk (task 2's contagion made local), bridge-employee identification (information layer), and informal-leader detection (cross-layer centrality). Risks and limitations: the other offices' layers do not exist yet, so the coupling is a design, not a measurement; trust and friendship surveys have response bias; the identity coupling is trivial here (one person, one node per layer) but the real value is in the inter-layer statistics, which require all layers to be current simultaneously; and the model's per-edge weights w_l are not calibrated in this work - they are the natural next calibration step once the friendship layer is measured. For the HR manager's vision, the practical first deliverable is the shared employee-key schema plus the friendship survey, because the churn-risk list is the fastest win and it uses only the HR outcome the office already has.
